paragraphs.text: Glucose phosphate isomerase (GPI) deficiency is an autosomal recessive cause of hereditary nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia. Patients have chronic hemolysis, with hemolytic crises during acute infections; severe cases may present with hydrops fetalis, and some patients have additional neurologic impairment. Splenectomy ameliorates the hemolysis. The deficient enzyme variants vary widely in their biochemical properties, and most are unstable (Arnold, 1979; Shalev et al., 1993; Kugler et al., 1998).

paragraphs.text: Hutton and Chilcote (1974) observed 8 children (5 living, 3 deceased) with severe hereditary nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia caused by GPI deficiency in 2 families from Kentucky and Indiana. All affected children were severely anemic in early life. The 3 deaths occurred in young patients who did not receive adequate blood transfusions or whose parents refused splenectomy. Splenectomy generally abolished the requirement for transfusion, and no patient required regular transfusion after puberty. Growth and development were surprisingly normal, and no patient died of infection. The abnormal enzyme was heat labile and was present in neutrophils and lymphocytes as well as erythrocytes.

paragraphs.text: Van Biervliet et al. (1975) described a new case of GPI deficiency in a Dutch family, designated GPI-Utrecht. In a separate report, Van Biervliet et al. (1975) described a new variant in which genetic and electrophoretic data pointed to a double heterozygous state in the patient.

paragraphs.text: Schroter et al. paragraphs.text: For discussion of the leu517-to-val (L517V) mutation in the GPI gene, resulting from a 1549C-G transversion, that was found together with the H389R mutation in 2 sibs with GPI deficiency without neurologic symptoms (GPI Calden) by Kugler et al. (1998), see GPI, HIS389ARG.

checks.claim: The GPI L517V mutation results from a 1549C-G transversion.
checks.explanation: Stated in the abstract. C>G is a transversion.

checks.claim: Kugler et al. (1998) found the GPI L517V mutation together with the H389R mutation in 2 sibs with GPI deficiency without neurologic symptoms (GPI Calden).
checks.evidence_quote: In the second family studied, the two affected siblings showed no neurological symptoms. The identified mutations are 1166 A-->G (H389R) and 1549 C-->G (L517V)

agent.process_note: I opened all 31 files. Twenty are abstracts only and 11 are titles only (5672849, 5673159, 5358143, 5782480, 5022716, 5025461, 4704861, 4611197, 4832160, 3796702, 8499925). For title-only papers I wrote nothing beyond what the title says, and I left out the two that don't bear on the human disorder or add nothing citable: Detter 1968 (inherited variation in phosphohexose isomerase) and Hutton 1969 (linkage in mice). I left out the Paglia and Valentine (1974) review as well. The only DNA-level variants in the folder are the four in Kugler et al. (1998); all the other reports describe enzyme variants biochemically. No reference data were supplied, and the papers never give a MIM number or chromosome location for the GPI gene, so I left both out of the intro. Kugler's abstract doesn't state the zygosity of the H389R/L517V pair in the GPI Calden family, so I didn't state it either. I also didn't claim that the GPI Homburg patient in Kugler is the same person Schroter et al. (1985) reported, because neither abstract says so.
